items.title: The Open Compute Project: Origins
items.transcript: Welcome to this OCP Academy course on Open Rack and ORv3. In this first lesson, we'll look at how the Open Compute Project began and how it shaped the Open Rack standard that so many modern data centers rely on today. The Open Compute Project, or OCP, was founded in 2011 by Facebook, now Meta, together with Intel and Rackspace. Their goal was to share open source hardware designs that could make data centers more efficient, scalable, and sustainable. The origins of Open Rack go back to Facebook's need to scale its infrastructure efficiently. Traditional data center designs were full of inefficiencies that added cost and complexity. The first Open Rack standard, called ORv1, launched in 2012 to 2013. Its centralized power distribution with a 12v DC power shelf and busbars. This reduced the number of server power cables and made racks easier to service. After ORv1, the community developed ORv2. It improved power and rack designs, but was mainly focused on hyperscale data centers, using 21 -inch servers and direct current power. This made it less common for wider enterprise use, which followed the traditional American Electronic Industries Alliance, EIA, standardized 19 -inch rack. By 2016, the community knew that new challenges like artificial intelligence and high -performance computing would require even higher power densities and better cooling. So development of ORv3 began. From 2016 to 2018, companies like Meta, Google, and Microsoft worked together to identify the need for higher power density, better cooling solutions, and more flexibility for both hyperscale and enterprise data centers. By 2019 and 2020, contributors like Advanced Energy were developing ORv3 power shelves that used a 48v DC architecture. This increased efficiency and supported more power -hungry workloads. In 2021, the OCP Global Summit showcased ORv3's readiness for broader adoption. Power shelves demonstrated 97 .5 % efficiency and up to 36kW in a 2OU form factor. By 2022, ORv3 was ready for full -scale deployment. ORv3 was designed to be flexible. It supports both 21 -inch open -compute equipment and older, standard 19 -inch equipment. It also includes features like liquid cooling manifolds and blindmate power connections to make installation easier. By 2024, adoption of ORv3 had grown significantly. Companies like Cheval, Eaton, Flex, Rittal, and Sanmina have their racks in the OCP marketplace based on the ORv3 specification. You'll even find racks from wooden data centers made from low -embedded carbon materials. In 2025, companies like Meta and NVIDIA contributed advanced designs such as the Catalina, an MGX AI rack, and Compute Shelf, which can handle up to 140kW per rack for powerful AI workloads. ORv3 has changed the data center industry by improving power efficiency, boosting cooling capabilities, and creating a more flexible open ecosystem. Today, the OCP continues to drive collaboration and standard specifications. Its open -source hardware approach helps data centers around the world scale for the future while staying efficient and sustainable with ever -increasing demands of higher performance computing to power artificial intelligence that, in turn, will boost the human intelligence behind every industry.

items.title: Inside the ORv3 Frame
items.transcript: Welcome to this detailed look inside the ORv3 frame. In this lesson, we'll identify the key physical specifications of Open Rack version 3, including its updated dimensions, the busbar system, and the power shelf that makes it so efficient for modern data centers. The ORv3 rack is the result of years of development work and collaboration between rack and component vendors, as well as the hyperscalers and wider OCP community. Over the last three years, this design has evolved to address the changing needs of high density, scalable data centers. Let's start at the front of the rack. One of the first physical features you'll notice is the new modular cable manager. This modular piece can be unscrewed and removed to allow for customized cable management across the entire aisle. Modular cable management gives operators the flexibility to organize cables neatly and adjust layouts as needs change, which helps with airflow and maintenance in large -scale deployments. Inside the rack frame, ORv3 can now accommodate both OU and RU shelves from top to bottom. In ORv2, there was only Open U positioning, but now standard rack units are supported too. This expanded shelf support means that operators can install more equipment with standard sizing, making the rack more versatile for different IT gear. Another key update is that these shelves are designed to be tool -less, saving time during installation. Now let's move to the back of the rack. One of the biggest improvements here is the upgraded busbar power system. In the previous version, ORv2 racks used a 12v busbar, but ORv3 has stepped up to a 48v system. This upgrade to 48v delivers higher power efficiency and greater capacity, which is crucial for AI and HPC workloads that require denser power distribution. The busbar is fully integrated into the rack frame, with easy access for connecting power shelves and IT gear. It's one of the core features that sets Open Rack apart from traditional designs. In addition to the busbar, ORv3 racks include features that future -proof the frame for advanced cooling. The frame has dedicated spaces to support cold -arm cooling manifolds when liquid cooling becomes more widely adopted. This means that as AI servers push power rack requirements higher, operators can switch from air cooling to liquid cooling without replacing the entire rack structure. Structurally, the ORv3 frame is built to handle heavy loads. Each rack can now dynamically support up to 1400kg, which has been tested and approved. This is an increase in strength and stability compared to previous designs. Having a higher load capacity means more equipment can be installed without compromising stability or airflow. This is especially important for data centers that are constantly upgrading or retrofitting equipment. All these features combined make the ORv3 rack more flexible, powerful, and ready for the demands of next -generation workloads. From its improved cable management to the upgraded busbar and shelf system, every design choice supports efficiency and scalability.

items.title: Cooling and Manifolds
items.transcript: In high -performance and AI -optimized data centers, thermal management is no longer just a matter of airflow. It's a fundamental design priority. The ORv3 specification integrates both air and liquid cooling support directly into the rack infrastructure, enabling flexibility across deployment types and workloads. Let's start with air cooling. ORv3 racks maintain compatibility with traditional air -cooled systems by supporting consistent front -to -rear airflow through the rack and chassis. This ensures that even legacy or mixed environment deployments remain viable, allowing a gradual transition to advanced cooling without a full infrastructure overhaul. However, as compute densities rise, especially in AI, HPC, and GPU -intensive environments, air alone isn't sufficient. That's where liquid cooling enters the frame. ORv3 introduces native support for Direct Liquid Cooling, or DLC, through a robust, blindmate manifold interface. This manifold sits at the back of the rack and serves as a shared thermal exchange interface for all DLC -compatible IT gear. A key feature is the rear blindmate connection. Each DLC -compatible sled or chassis is fitted with a cold plate interface that connects seamlessly to the manifold without requiring tools or human intervention. This allows for hot swapping of gear even in liquid -cooled environments, reducing service downtime and risk of leaks. The manifold itself is engineered for high flow capacity and thermal efficiency. It typically supports 12mm quick disconnect couplings, but the spec allows flexibility in connector design provided they meet OCP -compliant standards. It's also modular, enabling single or multi -loop configurations to accommodate variable thermal loads within the same rack. ORv3 also accommodates coolant distribution units, or CDUs, located externally or internally, depending on deployment. These CDUs circulate and manage coolant through the rack loop, often interfacing with facility -side cooling systems such as cooling towers or heat exchangers. Another ORv3 advantage is sustainability through higher thermal set points. By allowing safe operation at higher inlet temperatures, often in the 27°C to 32°C range, ORv3 racks reduce the energy needed for chilling, aligning with ASHRAE A1 standards and enabling broader use of free cooling or warm water cooling loops. Finally, air flow and liquid cooling are not mutually exclusive. Many ORv3 deployments adopt hybrid cooling strategies, combining air -cooled IT gear with liquid -cooled accelerators or GPUs in the same rack. The rack design supports this mixed configuration through flexible mounting and airflow containment options. Together, these cooling innovations make ORv3 a highly adaptable platform for future -ready thermal management. Whether you're operating traditional servers or AI clusters pushing 100 kW per rack,

items.title: Payload Options and Compatibility
items.transcript: Let's talk about payload compatibility. The flexibility of the ORv3 rack to support different types of IT equipment. This is a critical factor in any modern deployment, and ORv3 delivers on it. The heart of ORv3's flexibility lies in its ability to accommodate both OCP native gear and traditional EIA standard equipment. That means organizations can deploy 21 -inch wide OCP gear while still supporting legacy 19 -inch servers, switches, and other hardware. This dual compatibility is more than a convenience. It enables smoother transitions between old and new infrastructure. Operators can adopt open hardware standards gradually without needing to forklift their existing inventory. Let's start with OCP native gear. These systems are designed specifically for ORv3's 21 -inch internal bay. The added width allows for more efficient component layouts, higher airflow, and better cable routing, all within a standard 600 -millimeter rack footprint. On the flip side, ORv3 is also engineered to mount 19 -inch EIA equipment using standardized adapters. These adapter brackets, or conversion trays, allow legacy hardware to fit securely inside the wider frame, preserving alignment with airflow and mounting holes. Mounting flexibility extends to both full -width and half -width sleds. In a typical ORv3 deployment, you'll find combinations of full -width compute nodes, half -width storage sleds, or high -density AI accelerators, all within the same rack. The rack's internal rail system is designed to support these varied payload types without modification. That's especially valuable for hyperscale and enterprise teams experimenting with different IT loads or phasing in new workloads like AI inference or HPC clusters. Another benefit? Tool -less mounting. Like other aspects of ORv3, payload installation is designed to be quick and serviceable. Whether it's an OCP sled or EIA gear with brackets, IT teams can install and remove equipment without specialized tools. This hybrid -ready approach makes ORv3 a future -proof choice. As more operators adopt open hardware designs, they won't need to discard their existing EIA hardware. ORv3 provides a seamless bridge between the two ecosystems. In short, ORv3 doesn't force a choice. It welcomes innovation while respecting existing infrastructure. That adaptability is part of what makes it so widely adopted. It's open, it's efficient, and it's built for the real -world needs of today's data centers.

items.title: ORv3 in Practice: Case Studies
items.transcript: When it comes to deploying ORv3 in the real world, two major players, Meta and Google, have each taken unique approaches, reflecting their scale, data center infrastructure, and evolving workload demands. These exercise different options in the ORv3 -based specification. Let's start with Meta. Meta's implementation of ORv3 builds on the standard specifications, option one with key adaptations for high performance computing. Their rack design emphasizes high availability and mechanical consistency using standardized 21 -inch IT gear form factors. It can support 44 OU total or 47 RU total units in terms of its height for payloads. It enables streamlined airflow and simplified servicing across global facilities. Power is delivered via 48V busbars, and the design accommodates high power workloads with modularity for future growth. Meta's ORv3 racks also include extended monitoring capabilities and predictable front -to -back airflow profiles, helping their infrastructure support rapid scalability while managing thermal loads efficiently. An update to Meta's frame specification with also planned and later came with high power rack versions and Meta's Catalina project and OCP contribution. On the other hand, Google's implementation offers depth options of both 32 and 48 inches. It has an OCP compliant feature set. It's capable of integrating industry standard equipment designed for EIA 19 -inch racks as well as custom payloads that are up to 24 inches wide and even greater than 36 inches deep. Furthermore, it has a load rating of 3 ,000 pounds which is on par with ORv3 specification of approximately 1 ,400 kilograms. The Google ORv3 implementation provides rear accessible flexible cable management as well as the ability to integrate both 48 volt DC power distribution as well as AC PDUs. Finally, there are provisions for rear and front accessories as well as the option for rack level EMI containment. What unites both companies is their commitment to open standards and the scalability that ORv3 provides, whether the goal is performance, sustainability, or deployment speed. ORv3 allows organizations to standardize their mechanical and electrical infrastructure, adapt to liquid cooling, and support both AI and cloud native workloads. Their contributions are also reflected in the spec documents that help evolve the ORv3 standard. Meta, Google, and others continue to iterate on ORv3 through collaborative development and transparent publishing. From hyperscale data centers to AI ready deployments, ORv3 is already powering the backbone of modern compute.

items.title: High Power Racks Overview
items.transcript: As AI and high performance computing workloads continue to scale, the power and cooling demands of modern data centers are reaching unprecedented levels. The Open Compute Project's High Power Rack, or HPR, addresses this challenge by extending the ORv3 standard to meet next -generation power requirements, without disrupting the foundational modularity that makes ORv3 so scalable. The motivation behind HPR is clear. Standard ORv3 racks typically support up to 18 to 36 kilowatts per rack. But with dense GPU and AI -accelerated deployments, operators are now pushing toward 100 kilowatts and beyond, towards the 1 megawatt rack. This doubling of power density demands more than just bigger power supplies. It requires a rack ecosystem rethink. That's where HPR comes in. It retains the same physical envelope and mechanical alignment as the base ORv3 standard, meaning you don't have to redesign your data center layout. Instead, HPR introduces enhanced features inside the rack to safely deliver higher power and manage thermal output more efficiently. The cornerstone of the ORv3 that continues with the HPR design is its adoption of 48V direct power distribution. Carried through a higher current, deeper designed busbar systems supported by a new extension to the back of the frame. This approach not only supports more powerful IT gear, but also improves energy efficiency by reducing conversion losses. New busbar extensions and grounding enhancements ensure safety and compatibility with OCP's evolving electrical architecture. But delivering more power is only half the story. The HPR solution also addresses the thermal challenge by integrating blindmate liquid cooling manifolds. These front -accessible modular cooling interfaces support cold plate loops directly within the rack, making it easier to manage heat generated by high wattage components. The design reduces reliance on traditional air cooling, helping facilities scale without exceeding environmental or HVAC limits. Importantly, HPR achieves all of this while remaining part of the broader ORv3 family. It's not a standalone solution. It's a high -power extension of a standard already in global deployment. That means facilities can gradually adopt HPR elements as their workload demands increase, without replacing their entire infrastructure. HPR was well -introduced at the OCP Global Summit in 2024, to support 92 kW or more. But since then, it's quickly evolving within the rack and power OCP projects community, through multiple iterations, with plans to now go to 1600 roofline rack power. In short, the high -power rack represents OCP's vision of an AI -ready, thermally resilient, and energy -optimized future. It allows data centers to meet rising demands without sacrificing the open, interoperable principles that ORv3 is built on.

items.title: High Power Rack Technical Focus
items.transcript: AI is driving power requirements dramatically. Led by Meta, the OCP Rack and Power Projects community developed with HPR to meet this demand. HPR features a 6 -inch deeper and 65 -kilogram heavier rack, primarily to increase busbar capacity from 18 kilowatts to 92 -kilowatts minimum, and upgraded power shelves from 3 -kilowatts to 5 .5 -kilowatts PSUs, totaling 33 -kilowatts per shelf. HPR also improved grounding and added room for an extra power shelf, allowing for 3 power and 3 BBU shelves. AC whips transitioned from 20A to 30A in North America. Today's most recent plans for HPR go up to 8 power shelves. The HPR rack's mechanical structure is simple. We bolted a welded extension to the standard ORv3 frame using existing mounting points. This extension supports the deeper busbar, providing protection and grounding. All standard accessories like security doors and rear heat exchanges can be used. The extension also supports up to 6 AC cable whips with integrated cable management. To maintain structural integrity and accommodate the added weight, HPR adds ballast masses at the front of the frame to ensure stability and pass UL qualifications. When designing the busbar, we considered going wider, but to accommodate platform concerns, we went deeper instead, adding 125mm for a total depth of 190mm. This increased the busbar weight from 15kg to 80kg, necessitating more robust mounting features. Instead of two screws, we now use eight at the bottom and a bracket at the top, for four mounting points. Through simulations and thermal testing in 2024, the first iteration of HPR achieved 155kW from the rack, even though real -world applications might yield slightly less. To support the higher power, we upgraded to 30A AC whips for North America, while EU maintains the 32A IEC 309 standard with two plugs instead of one. Moving from ORV3 to ORV3 HPR also shifted the rack grounding point to the busbar side, connecting the 50V return and busbar cage with metal blocks. This allows us to remove IT gear input connector ground contacts. We also changed the busbar cage material to low -conductivity steels to increase contact resistance and mitigate potential ground current. The HPR power shelf, still 1U, now outputs 33kW with 5 .5kW PSUs. We upgraded busbar output connectors to 700A and designed dedicated thermistors to monitor busbar clip temperature. HPR PSUs significantly increased peak power capability, supporting 136 % rated power for 50ms and 160 % for 400 microseconds, crucial for GPU workloads. Finally, Bennett, together with its OCP community partners, developed an Active Power Monitoring Module, PMM, with an MCU for automatic address allocation and critical parameter consolidation. All our PSU, BBU, PMM, and AC Whips specs are available on the OCP Rack and Power Wiki, with the overall rack spec coming soon.

items.title: The AI Data Center 1 Megawatt Rack: ORv3’s Future
items.transcript: As data centers race to meet the exponential growth of AI workloads in AI factories powered in high megawatts and even gigawatts, electrical demands per rack are surging to levels once considered unthinkable to power much denser compute infrastructure. The industry is now preparing for a new benchmark, the one megawatt rack. ORv3 plays a central role in this transition. It provides a standardized foundation that can be extended to meet the needs of one megawatt rack deployments. The key is to retain the mechanical and interface consistency of ORv3 while allowing flexible enhancements that increase power and thermal capabilities without forcing a complete redesign. From a power perspective, the journey to one megawatt involves a few critical shifts. First, power must be delivered at higher voltages and through larger conductors, often in the form of overhead busways instead of traditional floor PDUs. These busways connect to high -capacity rectifiers, which then distribute power down through the racks via new high -current busbar extensions. At the rack level, internal distribution must be robust enough to handle up to 100 kilowatts or more per zone. Power shelves must support greater density and redundancy and racks must allow multiple feeds to deliver the necessary amperage safely. Throughout this architecture, grounding becomes a critical design point with careful attention paid to bonding paths, fault protection, and compliance with global safety standards. Microsoft, Meta, and Google have come together at the OCP to contribute a new way to distribute power, and thus enable the one megawatt IT rack by introducing a power rack. Instead of data center electrical busways feeding power shelves directly to the IT rack, taking up precious space that cannot be used for IT servers, this new approach implements a sidecar power rack. The sidecar rack is also based on ORV3 and high -voltage DC. This specification is named Mount Diablo, and it provides for options at 800 volts monopole DC or plus minus 400 volts, reusing the supply chain components from the electric vehicle industry. It receives the power from the facility power distribution, and then feeds it to the IT rack. Either directly to the bus bar pre -converted to 48 volts with a busbar clip connector, or an intermediate converter can be placed in the IT rack, which then feeds the bus bar at the lower voltage needed for servers. There is additional cable distribution and connector innovation required associated with the Diablo rack for safety and efficiency. But scaling power alone isn't enough, a one megawatt rack generates extreme heat. That's why liquid cooling, already part of ORV3's vision, is now a must. Cold plate loops, rear door heat exchangers, and facility water integration are all being designed as native features, not add -ons. Blindmate manifolds and front -access cooling interfaces make serviceability and safety manageable even at scale. Importantly, ORV3's open and modular architecture enables vendors and operators to adopt these innovations incrementally. A facility might start with 30 -kilowatt racks and gradually evolve toward 100 -kilowatt or more, while staying within the same rack standard. This allows for global interoperability, faster innovation, and shared learning across the OCP community. The one megawatt rack is no longer a concept, it's a necessity. ORV3 ensures that as we scale toward this future, we do so with standardization, safety, and sustainability in mind.

items.title: The Evolution of Open Rack: From ORv3 to ORW
items.transcript: For years, the ORW base has been the undisputed foundation of efficient data center infrastructure. But the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence has fundamentally changed the physical requirements of computing. Next generation AI workloads demand massive scale up networks and larger silicon footprints. Engineers need the physical space to distribute multiple GPUs evenly across the compute tray. This balanced distribution prevents severe thermal hotspots and optimizes complex network routing. Within the boundaries of a traditional 600 millimeter wide rack, these physical layouts become a severe bottleneck. The community needed a new standard. Enter the open rack wide or ORW. This new specification literally doubles the width of the standard rack to 1200 millimeters or in inches expanding from 21 to 42. This expansion allows engineers to build massive interconnected AI platforms without compromising on modularity, but this shift is about much more than just physical space. The transition to ORW is a necessary evolution toward high power racks. This wider format provides the crucial volume required to route complex liquid cooling manifolds, seamlessly integrate high power racks, shared baseline power shelves, and support the extreme payload weight of fully populated AI clusters. By anticipating the physical demands of next generation silicon, the Open Compute project ensures that scalability and efficiency remain available to everyone. Let's take a look inside the new frame.

items.title: ORW Cabling and Transport
items.transcript: The transition to the open rack wide introduces a massive new logistical challenge for facility operators. A fully populated ORW AI rack can easily weigh up to 3500 kg. At this extreme scale and beyond across multiple such racks, we are no longer just managing IT gear. We are managing heavy industry. Because of this immense weight, standard rolling casters are no longer a safe or viable option. The ORW frame eliminates casters entirely. The rack is designed to sit directly on structural platforms using dedicated pallet mounting brackets. This guarantees maximum stability and prevents catastrophic floor damage. Transporting a 3500 kg machine requires precision mechanization. The ORW base provides the specific clearances required for automated rack transport carts to safely lift, maneuver, and deploy the payload down the aisle. Once secured, operators must manage the massive data requirements of the AI cluster. The ORW frame incorporates spacious top and rear cable channels. These dedicated routing paths keep massive bundles of optical interconnects completely secure and safely out of the primary thermal exhaust path. By standardizing these transport and cabling interfaces, OCP ensures that deploying massive infrastructure remains safe, but standards like this are a continuous work in progress. Because there is still room for defining new standards for the next generation of heavy wide racks. We actively invite the community to participate in generating any missing specifications. Join the work group today to help shape the future of high density deployment.

items.title: ORW Cooling & Manifolds
items.transcript: We have built the structural frame and we have delivered the power. Now we must cool the system. With the open rack wide supporting extreme density AI clusters, advanced liquid cooling is a mandatory requirement. To manage the immense weight of the IT gear within the expanded 1200 millimeter width, ORW utilizes a unique mechanical substructure known as the canister. This heavily reinforced chassis ensures rigid support and precise alignment as the massive server nodes slide into the rack. This mechanical precision is absolutely critical. To extract the massive heat load. Thick vertical cooling manifolds are mounted securely into the expanded side channels of the ORW frame. Keeping the fluid completely separate from the central power delivery. Connecting a multi 100 pound server into these vertical manifolds requires absolute perfection. The solution is the pivoting blind mate coupling or PBMC. As the canister slides into the rack, the PBMC system automatically aligns the fluid connectors. It utilizes a brilliant mechanical pivot to absorb the extreme weight and positional tolerance of the hardware, ensuring a zero leak fluid lock without any manual intervention. The engineering behind this connection is a masterpiece of open hardware design. Let's take a closer look at exactly how the PBMC mechanism engages in our next interactive deep dive.

items.title: ORW in Practice: Case Studies
items.transcript: The open rack wide is no longer just a design specification. The OCP ecosystem is actively building and deploying this massive infrastructure to power the next generation of artificial intelligence. Today, we are looking at how the industry brings this architecture to life. To accelerate adoption, engineering teams develop internal reference solutions to prove the architecture at scale. A prime example is the AMD Helios AI rack, which is built on foundational OCP designs originally contributed. By Meta and Ridal, Helios serves as a highly optimized reference instantiation of the ORW specification. By looking at the Helios compute trays, you can see the true value of the 1200 millimeter width. The design showcases how larger AI accelerators, closely and efficiently packed scale-up networking, expansive memory configuration, and liquid cooling manifolds all integrate seamlessly with a single continuous chassis. But the open hardware ecosystem thrives on adaptation. Partners take these reference designs and deliver fully realized turnkey commercial solutions. For example, the HPE co-branded Helios deployment combines 72 AMD instinct GPUs with purpose-built Ethernet scale-out networking and advanced direct liquid cooling. And with new ORW implementations from partners like Super Micro being announced, the market for ORW infrastructure is expanding rapidly. From reference designs to massive commercial deployments, the Open Rack Wide is actively reshaping the modern data center. But AI is moving fast, and next, we will explore the extreme megawatt trends pushing this hardware to its absolute limits.
